options: Throughput: one instruction finishes per cycle instead of one every four
Latency: each instruction completes faster
Both, in proportion to the number of stages
Lower power, by keeping stages idle
drills.why: Any individual instruction takes as long as it did, or slightly longer. It is the same trade as the pipelined adder in unit 016 at a different scale.

options: Not knowing which instruction comes next until a branch resolves
Two instructions needing the same execution unit
An instruction needing a result that is not ready
An interrupt arriving mid-instruction
drills.why: By the time the condition is computed, the pipeline would like to have fetched a dozen more instructions. Guessing is the answer.

options: False dependencies from reusing register names
The need to save registers across calls
Cache conflicts between registers and memory
The limit on how many registers an instruction may name
drills.why: It is why having only sixteen architectural registers is less crippling than it sounds: there are far more physical ones underneath.

drills.q: Roughly what does a branch misprediction cost?
options: About fifteen to twenty cycles, roughly the pipeline depth
One cycle
About two hundred cycles, like a memory fetch
It depends on how many instructions the branch skipped
drills.why: Everything fetched after the branch is discarded and fetching restarts. So the cost of a branch is the misprediction rate times twenty, not the branch.

drills.q: Why does sorting an array before a loop that tests each element make the loop faster?
options: The condition becomes predictable, so the branch stops being mispredicted
Sorted data has better cache locality
The compiler can vectorise sorted loops
It does not; the instruction count is identical
drills.why: The instruction count is identical, which is exactly what makes this the classic demonstration.

drills.q: Why does a two-bit counter beat a one-bit one?
options: A single exception moves it without flipping the prediction, so a loop exit costs one miss rather than two
It can represent four outcomes instead of two
It updates faster
It tolerates alternating patterns
drills.why: Alternating patterns defeat it entirely. What two bits buy is tolerance of one unusual iteration in a long run.

drills.q: Why does saturation matter in the counter?
options: Without it, a long run drives the value far from the threshold and many contrary branches are needed to change its mind
Without it the counter overflows and wraps to the opposite prediction
It makes the update cheaper in hardware
It prevents the predictor from being trained by an attacker
drills.why: Measured: on twelve taken branches followed by six not-taken, a saturating counter mispredicts three times and an unbounded one mispredicts seven.

drills.q: What does speculation leave behind when it is discarded?
options: Cache lines it brought in, whose presence is visible through timing
Register values that were not restored
Memory writes that were committed early
Nothing; the rollback is complete
drills.why: That is Spectre. Undoing the architectural state was never the same as undoing all the state, which is how a 1990s optimisation became a 2018 security problem.

drills.q: Why is a reduction loop written with several accumulators?
options: Independent chains let the adder start a new operation every cycle instead of every fourth
It reduces the number of additions
It improves cache locality of the accumulator
It allows the compiler to use wider registers
drills.why: Same arithmetic, different dependency shape. In a loop accumulating a million values it is typically a factor of four.

drills.q: Why can the compiler not split a floating point reduction for you?
options: Reassociating changes the rounding and therefore the specified result
It cannot prove the accumulators do not alias
The standard requires a single accumulator
It can, and does, at -O2
drills.why: Three groupings of the same eight values gave 16777224, 16777216 and 16777222 in this unit's exercise. All three are correct arithmetic.

options: Permission to assume no infinities and no not-a-numbers
Use of hardware transcendental instructions
Lower precision for intermediate results only
Automatic vectorisation of every loop
drills.why: It grants rather more than most people intend, which is how it turns some correct code into wrong code silently.

drills.q: How many 32-bit floats fit in a 512-bit vector register?
options: Sixteen
Eight
Four
Sixty-four
drills.why: Eight at 256 bits and four at 128. An element count that is not a multiple of the width leaves a scalar tail.

drills.q: Why does a possible pointer overlap prevent vectorisation?
options: A write in one iteration could change a read in the next, so the iterations are not independent
Overlapping ranges cannot be loaded into vector registers
The compiler cannot compute the trip count
It does not; overlap only affects correctness, not vectorisation
drills.why: An optimiser needs a proof rather than a probability. restrict supplies the proof, and keeping the promise then becomes yours.

drills.q: An instruction has four-cycle latency and one-per-cycle throughput. When does the latency matter?
options: Only when the next operation needs the previous answer
Always; four cycles is four cycles
Never, since the unit is pipelined
Only when the operands come from memory
drills.why: A million multiplies into one accumulator is four million cycles. The same million across four accumulators is one million.

drills.q: What keeps the sequential illusion intact under out-of-order execution?
options: Retiring instructions in program order, whatever order they executed in
Executing only instructions whose operands are ready
The reorder buffer's size limit
Memory barriers inserted by the compiler
drills.why: The processor keeps a window, executes whatever is ready, and puts the results back in order so the outside world sees a sequential machine.
